title: Designing a Least Recently Used Cache

phrases.explanation: A rule that decides which item to remove when the cache is full
An operation that always takes the same amount of time regardless of data size
A compromise where gaining one thing requires giving up another
To explain something step by step

technical_terms.definition: A cache that removes the least recently used item first when it reaches capacity
A linked list where each node has pointers to both the next and previous nodes
A data structure that maps keys to values with average O(1) lookup time
A Java map that maintains insertion or access order of entries
A dummy node used at the boundary of a linked list to simplify edge case handling

java_methods.description: Returns the value mapped to the given key, or null if not present
Inserts or updates a key-value pair in the map
Removes the mapping for the specified key
Override this method to define a policy for automatically removing the oldest entry

concept: Design a data structure that follows the Least Recently Used eviction policy. It should support get and put operations, both in O(1) time. When the cache exceeds its capacity, it should invalidate the least recently used item before inserting a new one.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Array and Linear Search
solutions.summary: Store entries in an array with timestamps. On each get or put, scan the entire array to find the key or the least recently used entry.

solutions.label: HashMap plus Doubly Linked List
solutions.summary: Combine a HashMap for O(1) key lookup with a doubly linked list to track usage order. Move accessed nodes to the front and evict from the tail.

solutions.label: Java LinkedHashMap
solutions.summary: Use Java's built-in LinkedHashMap with access-order mode and override removeEldestEntry to automatically evict when capacity is exceeded.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style P fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style C fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    P["LRU Cache\ncapacity = 2"] --> OP1["put(1, 'A')"]
    OP1 --> OP2["put(2, 'B')"]

    OP4 --> C["Key 2 evicted\n(least recently used)"]

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Let's say you need to design a cache with a fixed capacity. It should support two operations: get and put. When the cache is full and you insert a new entry, it must remove the least recently used item. Both operations should run in constant time.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I see. So just to confirm, the cache maps integer keys to integer values, and we're given the capacity at construction time. What should get return if the key doesn't exist?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Return negative one if the key is not found. Also, calling get on an existing key counts as a use, so it updates that item's recency.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. And for put, if the key already exists, we update the value and mark it as recently used. If the key is new and the cache is at capacity, we evict the least recently used entry first. Let me walk through an example: with capacity two, we put key one then key two. Then we get key one, making it most recent. Now when we put key three, key two gets evicted since it's the least recently used.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's exactly right. Go ahead and start with any approach that comes to mind.

sections.title: Brute Force with Array and Linear Search
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SCAN fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    S["Array of entries\n(key, value, timestamp)"] --> PUT1["put(1,'A') ts=1\n[(1,'A',1)]"]
    PUT1 --> PUT2["put(2,'B') ts=2\n[(1,'A',1),(2,'B',2)]"]
    PUT2 --> GET1["get(1) ts=3\nScan array → found\nUpdate ts to 3"]
    GET1 --> PUT3["put(3,'C') ts=4\nCache full!"]
    PUT3 --> SCAN["Scan for min ts\nKey 2 has ts=2 → evict"]
    SCAN --> RES["[(1,'A',3),(3,'C',4)]"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: My first thought is a simple approach. I'll store entries in an array where each entry holds a key, value, and a timestamp. Each time we access or insert, we increment the timestamp. For get, I scan the array to find the key, which takes O of n time.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And what about eviction when the cache is full?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: When the array is at capacity, I scan all entries to find the one with the smallest timestamp. That's the least recently used item, so I remove it and insert the new one. Both get and put require a linear scan, giving us O of n time per operation.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. This works but doesn't meet the constant time requirement. Can you do better?

sections.title: HashMap plus Doubly Linked List
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style HM fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style HEAD fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style TAIL fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    HM["HashMap\n1→Node1\n3→Node3"] -.-> HEAD
    HEAD["Head\n(dummy)"] <--> N1["Node1\nkey=1, val='A'"]
    N1 <--> N3["Node3\nkey=3, val='C'"]
    N3 <--> TAIL["Tail\n(dummy)"]
    style N1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The bottleneck in the brute force is searching and finding the least recent item. I can solve both with a combination of a HashMap and a doubly linked list. The HashMap maps each key to its corresponding node in the linked list, giving us O of one lookup.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The doubly linked list maintains the usage order. The most recently used node sits right after the head sentinel, and the least recently used node sits right before the tail sentinel. I'll use dummy head and tail nodes to avoid null checks at the boundaries.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How do get and put work with this structure?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: For get, I look up the key in the HashMap. If found, I unlink the node from its current position and re-insert it right after the head. For put, if the key exists, I update the value and move the node to the front. If it's new and we're at capacity, I remove the node just before the tail, which is the least recently used, delete it from the HashMap, then add the new node at the front. Everything is O of one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. This is the classic approach interviewers expect. Is there a way to simplify the implementation in Java?

sections.title: Java LinkedHashMap
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style LHM fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style OV fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    LHM["LinkedHashMap\naccess-order = true\ncapacity = 2"] --> PUT1["put(1,'A')\nOrder: [1]"]
    PUT1 --> PUT2["put(2,'B')\nOrder: [1, 2]"]
    PUT2 --> GET1["get(1)\nOrder: [2, 1]"]
    GET1 --> PUT3["put(3,'C')"]
    PUT3 --> OV["removeEldestEntry\nsize 3 > 2 → evict key 2"]
    OV --> RES["Order: [1, 3]"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Java actually has a built-in class called LinkedHashMap that combines a HashMap with a doubly linked list internally. If I set the access-order flag to true in the constructor, it automatically reorders entries on each get call.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Then I override the removeEldestEntry method to return true when the size exceeds the capacity. This makes the map automatically evict the eldest entry on each put. The entire LRU cache becomes just a few lines of code, with O of one for both operations.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's clean and practical. In a real interview, knowing this approach shows familiarity with the standard library. But be prepared to explain the underlying mechanism if asked.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Absolutely. Under the hood, LinkedHashMap does exactly what we built manually: a hash table for fast lookup and a doubly linked list for ordering. The key insight is that both data structures work together to achieve constant time for every operation.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. We started with a brute force array scan at O of n time, then achieved O of one using a HashMap combined with a doubly linked list, and finally simplified the code using Java's LinkedHashMap.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The core takeaway is that combining a hash map with a doubly linked list is the standard pattern for any problem requiring both fast lookup and ordering. It's a powerful trade-off of extra space for constant time operations.
